# Introduction {#intro}

*Why should a crease pattern tell you anything about a gene expression matrix?*

It should not, and this book does not claim that it does. A folded sheet of
paper is not a model of transcription, and no argument here depends on
pretending otherwise.

The claim is narrower, and in exchange it is checkable. The things we point at
a gene expression matrix — PCA, Isomap, t-SNE, UMAP, an autoencoder, and the
scores used to grade their output — are instruments. Instruments are calibrated
against a standard whose value is known, not against the specimen you are
curious about. A rigid crease pattern is such a standard. It is a manifold
whose correct two-dimensional description is available in closed form, at any
sample size, at a difficulty you can turn up continuously with one parameter.
Point an instrument at it and the reading can be compared with the truth
instead of with an expectation.

That is the whole trick, and the rest of this book is what follows from it.

## A crease pattern is the answer key {#intro-answer-key}

Rigid origami folds a flat sheet along creases while every facet stays flat
[@demaine2007folding]. Nothing stretches, nothing tears, and the material
between creases does not bend. The map from the flat sheet to the folded
surface is therefore an isometry: lengths measured *along* the surface are
identical before and after folding. Chapter \@ref(folding-geometry) develops
the geometry; @hull2020origametry is the standard reference.

The consequence is worth stating slowly, because everything else rests on it.

Take a point on the folded surface $\mathcal{M} \subset \mathbb{R}^3$. It came
from exactly one point on the flat sheet $\mathcal{U} \subset \mathbb{R}^2$.
That flat coordinate is a two-dimensional description of the point, and the
unfolding $\phi : \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{U}$ satisfies

$$
d_{\mathcal{M}}(p, q) \;=\; \lVert \phi(p) - \phi(q) \rVert_2
\qquad \text{for all } p, q \in \mathcal{M},
$$

where $d_{\mathcal{M}}$ is geodesic distance along the folded surface. The
sheet is a convex domain, so the straight segment joining any two flat
coordinates stays inside it and the identity holds globally, not merely for
nearby points.

No numerical approximation appears anywhere in that statement. $\mathcal{U}$ is
not a good embedding, not a defensible embedding, not the embedding a
well-tuned method converges to given enough compute. It *is* the embedding,
unique up to a rigid motion of the plane — and that residual freedom is exactly
what Procrustes alignment removes before any error is measured.

So the object under study comes with its own answer key, and the key is not a
proxy for the truth, a consensus of methods, or a label someone assigned by
eye. It is the generating coordinate itself, returned by the constructor before
any folding happens.

```{r intro-answer-key-demo}
library(foldbenchR)

# A Miura-ori sheet: 4 by 6 parallelogram cells.
pattern <- miura_ori(n_rows = 4, n_cols = 6, a = 1, b = 1, alpha = pi / 3)

# The exact flat embedding. No inference, no optimisation, no fitting.
head(unfold(pattern))

# Sample the folded surface with a little ambient measurement noise.
# theta is the fold angle, in radians, bounded above by pi/2.
s <- sample_manifold(
  pattern,
  theta = pi / 6,
  n     = 2000,
  noise = list(type = "ambient", sd = 0.01),
  seed  = BENCH_SEEDS[1]
)

dim(s$X)      # 2000 x 3  — what any method is allowed to see
dim(s$truth)  # 2000 x 2  — the exact flat coordinates that produced X
```

`s$truth` is not an estimate. It is the argument that was passed to the fold
map, recovered without inference. Any embedding $Y$ of `s$X` can therefore be
scored against it directly:

```{r intro-scoring}
Y <- prcomp(s$X, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)$x[, 1:2]

reconstruction_error(Y, s$truth)        # how far PCA is from the truth
reconstruction_error(s$truth, s$truth)  # 0, by construction — the ruler's zero
```

The second line looks trivial. It is the point. On a real dataset there is no
second line, and every quantity reported is a distance from something that is
itself uncertain.

## Exact geodesics, for free {#intro-geodesics}

The isometry buys something beyond the embedding, and it is worth making
explicit because a whole family of methods is built to estimate it.

Isomap [@tenenbaum2000isomap] works by approximating geodesic distance on the
data manifold with shortest paths through a $k$-nearest-neighbour graph. That
approximation is the method's central assumption and its principal failure
mode. On a crease pattern, no approximation is required: because folding
preserves along-surface length, the ordinary Euclidean distance matrix of the
flat truth *is* the exact geodesic distance matrix of the folded surface.

```{r intro-geodesics-demo}
# Exact geodesic distances on the folded surface in R^3 — computed in R^2,
# because folding does not change them.
G <- dist(s$truth)
```

One line, no graph, no shortest-path search, no neighbourhood parameter to
tune. So the error in Isomap's geodesic estimate is itself measurable, which is
a strictly stronger position than being able to measure only the error of its
final embedding. Chapter \@ref(geodesic) uses this to separate the two failures
that are usually conflated: a bad geodesic estimate, and a bad embedding of
good geodesics.

Figure \@ref(fig:intro-fold-sweep) shows what the fold angle $\theta$ does to
the sheet. At $\theta = 0$ the manifold is a plane and PCA is exact. As $\theta$
rises the accordion compresses, points on facets that are far apart on the
sheet approach each other in $\mathbb{R}^3$, and the two-dimensional structure
gets progressively harder to recover — continuously, with no discontinuity
anywhere in the generating process. Every distance in `G` is unchanged
throughout.

```{r intro-fold-sweep, fig.cap = "One Miura-ori sheet at four fold angles, seen in profile. Difficulty is a dial, not a fixed dataset.", fig.alt = "Four side-by-side scatter panels showing the profile of the same folded sheet in the ambient y-z plane at fold angles 0, 0.5, 1.0 and 1.4 radians. At theta = 0 the points lie on a single horizontal line of width about 4 units. As theta increases the line opens into a zigzag: the horizontal extent shrinks to under 1 unit while the vertical extent grows to about 1 unit, so facets that are far apart along the sheet end up close together in ambient space. Up-sloping and down-sloping facets are distinguished by both colour and point shape."}
library(ggplot2)

thetas <- c(0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.4)   # radians; the fold is defined on [0, pi/2)

sweep <- do.call(rbind, lapply(thetas, function(th) {
  m <- sample_manifold(pattern, theta = th, n = 400, seed = BENCH_SEEDS[1])
  # Facet band is a function of the exact truth, not of the ambient data.
  band <- floor(m$truth[, "y"] / pattern$params$b)
  data.frame(
    y     = m$X[, "y"],
    z     = m$X[, "z"],
    slope = factor(band %% 2, levels = 0:1,
                   labels = c("up-sloping", "down-sloping")),
    theta = sprintf("theta == %.2f", th)
  )
}))

ggplot(sweep, aes(y, z, colour = slope, shape = slope)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ theta, nrow = 1, labeller = label_parsed) +
  scale_color_book(name = "facet") +
  scale_shape_manual(name = "facet", values = c(16, 17)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "ambient y", y = "ambient z") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```

A fair objection arrives immediately: the Swiss roll also has a known
parameterisation [@tenenbaum2000isomap], so what has been gained? Four things.
The crease pattern is a *family* indexed by $\theta$ rather than a single
geometry, so no configuration can be quietly selected after the fact. Its
geodesics are exact rather than estimated, as above. It is piecewise flat, so
it violates the smoothness assumptions that manifold-learning theory leans on —
a feature, since real data manifolds have creases too. And it composes:
products of folded sheets give exact ground truth at intrinsic dimension $2k$,
where a benchmark stuck at dimension 2 cannot go. Chapter \@ref(comparison)
runs the head-to-head and reports where the two benchmarks disagree about
method rankings.

## What is claimed {#intro-claims}

Four claims, in decreasing order of confidence.

**One.** For a rigidly folded crease pattern, the flat pattern is the exact
two-dimensional embedding. This is geometry, not an empirical finding, and it
is either true or the fold is not rigid.

**Two.** Because the truth is exact, reconstruction error is a *measurement*.
Procrustes-aligned RMSE against $\mathcal{U}$ has a known zero, a known scale,
and no dependence on the method being graded. Chapter \@ref(evaluation) makes
this the headline metric.

**Three.** The same exactness lets us audit the metrics that are used when no
truth exists. Trustworthiness, continuity and $k$-nearest-neighbour
preservation are all surrogates for a distortion nobody can normally observe.
Here the distortion is observable, so the surrogates can be scored on how well
they track it. This is the book's main experimental contribution.

**Four.** The resulting rankings sometimes disagree with rankings obtained from
the standard benchmarks, and a benchmark that never changes a decision is not
worth running. Chapter \@ref(application) tests whether it changes one.

## What is not claimed {#intro-not-claimed}

A folded sheet is not a cell. Nothing here establishes that any biological
dataset lies near a developable surface, and no result should be read as
evidence about the geometry of transcriptomes. The generalisation runs the
other way: a method that cannot recover a two-dimensional structure whose truth
is exact and whose noise you specified yourself has not earned the benefit of
the doubt on data where the truth is unknown. Failure here is informative.
Success here is necessary, not sufficient.

Nor is this a claim that low-dimensional visualisation should be abandoned.
Measuring distortion is not the same as concluding that the distortion is
fatal, and this book takes no position on that beyond what its own numbers
support.

Finally, none of this is a contribution to rigidity theory or to computational
origami design. The patterns used are textbook ones — Miura-ori, Yoshimura,
waterbomb [@lang2011origami] — chosen because their fold kinematics are known
in closed form and cheap to compute, not because they are novel.

## The target {#intro-target}

@chari2023specious argue that two-dimensional embeddings of single-cell
genomics data are systematically misleading: that the pictures preserve far
less of the original high-dimensional relationships than their use in the
literature assumes, that the distortion is intrinsic to the compression rather
than a tuning failure, and that conclusions read off such pictures are
therefore unsafe. The rebuttals — that careful initialisation, perplexity and
neighbourhood choices recover much of the structure [@kobak2019art] — are
serious, but both sides argue on terrain where nobody has the answer key. On a
gene expression matrix there is no $\mathcal{U}$ to compare against. The debate
is conducted with surrogates on both sides.

That is not a rhetorical complaint. It has a concrete cost: when two groups
report different trustworthiness scores for the same embedding pipeline, there
is no third quantity either can appeal to. Disagreements about the *method*
become indistinguishable from disagreements about the *ruler*, and the
literature has no mechanism for telling them apart.

This book takes that challenge as its target, and accepts a strict limit on
what it can do about it. It cannot tell you whether any particular UMAP plot of
any particular tissue is misleading. It can tell you how much distortion a
given method introduces on a manifold of specified difficulty, where "how much"
is a number with units and a known zero. And — more usefully for the argument —
it can tell you whether the instruments both camps use to make their case are
reporting that distortion faithfully.

## Evaluating the evaluators {#intro-evaluators}

Here is the move that exact truth makes available, and which no standard
benchmark supports.

A metric such as trustworthiness takes the ambient data $X$ and the embedding
$Y$ and returns a score in $[0, 1]$. It is used as a stand-in for the true
distortion, which is normally unobservable. When $\mathcal{U}$ is known, both
quantities are available at once, and the surrogate can be scored on how well
it tracks what it stands in for — across methods, across fold angles, across
noise levels, across seeds.

The sharpest diagnostic is the cheapest one: evaluate the metrics on the truth
itself.

```{r intro-metric-on-truth}
trustworthiness(s$X,  s$truth, k = 15)   # the exact answer does not score 1
knn_preservation(s$X, s$truth, k = 15)
```

Neither returns 1, and $k$-nearest-neighbour preservation is not close to it.
It cannot be, because these metrics compare neighbourhoods in the *ambient*
data — which contain measurement noise, and, once the sheet is folded far
enough, short circuits between facets that lie close in $\mathbb{R}^3$ but far
apart on the sheet — against neighbourhoods in the embedding. The correct
unfolding deliberately separates points that the ambient geometry has pushed
together, and the metric charges it for doing so.

The consequence is uncomfortable and easy to state: a method can score *higher*
than the truth. On this sheet with two-dimensional PCA, across all 20 benchmark
seeds, it always does — at a flat $\theta = 0$ and at a nearly compressed
$\theta = 1.5$ alike. In the compressed case PCA collapses the fold entirely,
which is close to the worst reconstruction available, and it still beats the
exact unfolding on $k$-nearest-neighbour preservation by a wide margin.
Whatever it is being rewarded for, it is not correctness. It is agreement with
the ambient artefacts that the fold created. Chapter \@ref(evaluation)
quantifies the gap across the full grid and reports how large it gets, for
which metrics, and at which fold angles.

There is a second reason the audit matters. Trustworthiness, continuity and
$k$-nearest-neighbour preservation are all built from the same object — the
$k$-neighbourhood graph — and Kruskal stress is dominated by the same short
distances. They are not four independent opinions. When they agree, the
agreement is weak evidence, because a distortion that the neighbourhood graph
cannot see is invisible to all of them at once. Exact truth is what turns that
suspicion into a measurement: Chapter \@ref(evaluation) reports how much of the
variance in the surrogates is shared, and how much of the true error none of
them captures.

That result is the reason the book is organised around a benchmark rather than
a method comparison. Comparing methods with a broken ruler produces a
confidently wrong ordering, and the ordering looks no less confident for being
wrong.

## The shape of the argument {#intro-roadmap}

**Part I — Folding.** Build the object. Chapter \@ref(folding-geometry)
establishes what makes a crease pattern a valid manifold: developability,
Maekawa's and Kawasaki's conditions, and why only *rigid* folding preserves the
isometry that everything depends on. Chapter \@ref(generative) turns one
pattern into a family — the Miura-ori parameterisation, uniform sampling on
facets, noise models, and what $\theta$ does to the $k$-nearest-neighbour graph.

**Part II — Methods under test.** Four families, each against exact truth.
Linear projections in Chapter \@ref(linear), where two components are exact at
$\theta = 0$ and the collapse of explained variance as $\theta$ rises motivates
everything after it. Geodesic methods in Chapter \@ref(geodesic): classical
MDS, Isomap [@tenenbaum2000isomap], locally linear embedding
[@roweis2000lle] — Isomap is *built* for isometric embeddings, so the
informative question is the exact angle at which its graph first bridges two
facets, which `foldbenchR` locates directly. Neighbour embeddings in Chapter
\@ref(neighbor), where t-SNE [@vandermaaten2008tsne] and UMAP
[@mcinnes2018umap] are separated from their own seed noise. Autoencoders in
Chapter \@ref(autoencoders), the only family that learns an explicit inverse,
which makes the fold–unfold identity directly computable.

**Part III — The benchmark.** Chapter \@ref(benchmarks) is the construction
proper: the `foldbenchR` API end to end, pattern families beyond Miura-ori,
product manifolds at intrinsic dimension $2k$, and random orthonormal lifts to
arbitrary ambient dimension. Chapter \@ref(evaluation) audits the evaluators.
Chapter \@ref(results) reports the full method $\times$ pattern $\times$
$\theta$ $\times$ noise grid as distributions, and states plainly how much
between-method variation falls inside within-method seed variance. Chapter
\@ref(comparison) asks whether any of this beats the Swiss roll.

**Part IV — Application.** Chapter \@ref(application) takes the grid, uses it
to choose a method and its hyperparameters, applies that choice to a real
single-cell dataset, and compares it against the field default. If the
benchmark-guided choice does not win, that is the result, and it is reported as
such. A benchmark whose recommendations are never tested against a real
decision is a simulation study with better marketing.

## What would falsify this {#intro-falsification}

The book's central claim is not a matter of taste, so it should be possible to
say what would sink it.

If the standard metrics turned out to track true reconstruction error closely
across the whole grid — high rank correlation with Procrustes RMSE at every
fold angle, every noise level, every pattern family — then exact truth would be
an elegant confirmation of what practitioners already do, and Chapter
\@ref(evaluation) would be a short chapter. If method rankings on crease
patterns matched rankings on the Swiss roll, Chapter \@ref(comparison) would
conclude that the new benchmark adds nothing and should not be used. If the
benchmark-guided choice in Chapter \@ref(application) lost to the default, the
practical case would collapse regardless of how clean the geometry is.

All three are live possibilities, and each is checked in the chapter that could
fail it. The argument for building this benchmark is that these questions have
answers, and that on a folded sheet the answers can be computed rather than
debated.
